Things I built

A small car with a real car's wiring

A Raspberry Pi sees the lane, traffic lights and stop signs. It never touches a motor. Three STM32 ECUs do the sensing, driving and display, and they all talk over one CAN bus, the way a real vehicle splits its electronics.

  • 4 nodes on one bus
  • 500 kbps CAN, 11-bit IDs
  • 500 ms safety watchdog
  • 0.36 ms mean command/feedback round trip over 100 tests
  • STM32F103, Raspberry Pi, SocketCAN, OpenCV, Embedded C, Python

Time since last safety frame (0x100), limit 500 ms

[FSM] DRIVING

Rules the Motor ECU follows: an unsafe 0x100 stops the motors at once. No 0x100 for 500 ms also stops them. After recovery it waits for a fresh 0x200 command, so an old command is never replayed.

Encoder feedback is used for RPM monitoring and fault checks. A closed-loop speed controller is the next step.

How this network was specified and tested before and after the boards were wired: HIL with CANoe.

Proved in CANoe, then on real ECUs

My In-Vehicle Networking capstone. The robot's CAN network was specified and tested in Vector CANoe first, then the same tests were run against real ECUs on a physical bus.

Four ECUs, one safety rule: the Motor ECU obeys a command only while the Sensor ECU's latest status is SAFE and less than 500 ms old. I built the whole network in CANoe before writing any firmware, wrote 19 automated tests against 13 requirements, and then reran those 19 tests unchanged on two STM32 boards and a laptop.

  • 19 / 19 tests pass in simulation and on hardware
  • 0 error frames in the final hardware regressions
  • 0.002 ms SD on the real ECUs' 100 ms cycles
  • 15 to 67 ms from a stimulus to UNSAFE on the real bus
  • 0.80 % bus load at 500 kbit/s
  • Vector CANoe 19, CAPL, CANdb++, Panel Designer, VN5620A, STM32 HAL, Python

    The interlock, in CAPL

    From my Motor_ECU.can model. The STM32 firmware follows the same rules.

    on message Safety_Status            /* 0x100: refresh watchdog, stop if UNSAFE */
{
  sensorSafety = this.Safety_State;
  watchdogOk   = 1;
  cancelTimer(tWatchdog);
  setTimer(tWatchdog, WATCHDOG_MS);
  if (sensorSafety != 0) StopMotors(ST_SAFETY);
}

on timer tWatchdog                  /* no 0x100 for 500 ms */
{
  watchdogOk = 0;
  StopMotors(ST_WATCHDOG);
  setTimer(tWatchdog, WATCHDOG_MS);
}

on message Motor_Command            /* 0x200: execute only if SAFE and fresh */
{
  if ((sensorSafety == 0) && (watchdogOk == 1))
  {
    appliedL   = Clamp100((int)this.Left_Cmd.phys);
    appliedR   = Clamp100((int)this.Right_Cmd.phys);
    motorState = ST_NORMAL;
  }
  else { appliedL = 0; appliedR = 0; }
}

    A SAFE status never restarts the motors on its own. Every stop is latched, and the ECU also starts latched, so the wheels move only on a new command received while SAFE.

    On the bench, sensor values come from CANoe and wheel speed comes from a model in the Motor ECU firmware. The Display ECU is still a CAPL node, and the ADAS ECU is a Python process on a laptop. Next: real sensor drivers and encoders, a Raspberry Pi and a TFT Display ECU, each checked with the same 19 tests.

    12 V in, 5 V out, and it has to stay 5 V

    I built a synchronous buck converter from a gate driver, two MOSFETs and an STM32, then wrote two controllers for it. A textbook dual-loop PI, and a sliding mode controller whose surface includes the inductor resistance and capacitor ESR.

    • 100 kHz PWM from TIM1
    • 10 kHz current loop, 1 kHz voltage loop in ISRs
    • ±50 mV with SMC under load and input steps
    • STM32F103, IR2104, INA240, MATLAB/Simulink

    A safety controller, designed before it was coded

    A bidirectional collision-avoidance system built in Simulink, Stateflow and Simscape. Ultrasonic distances drive a state machine that slows or stops two modelled DC motors, and Simulink Coder turns it into C.

    • 342 blocks
    • 100% decision coverage
    • Model Advisor warnings 29 → 1
    • C99 code generated with Simulink Coder
